sentences.text: She had said it to Marta, at the far end of the hornbeams, in the second week of April, and she had said it in a temper, and it had been about Marta's father.
She is not going to write down what it was.

It was not a secret and it was not a lie; it was a true thing about a difficult situation that everybody in the village knew and nobody in the village said, and Iva had said it, out loud, at some volume, to the one person on earth who should not have had to hear it.
Marta had gone home.
They had made it up by about the following Tuesday in the way twelve-year-olds do, which is to say entirely and without ever referring to it.

And then in June Iva had found a web, and by August she had worked out what it did, and by the first of September she had spent three weeks understanding that in about ten days the entire village was going to walk up that path through a wash of everything said under those trees since March.
She did not sleep well.

She considered, seriously, going up there and taking the web down early, and she got as far as the third hornbeam with a stick before she worked out that she had no idea whether that would empty it slowly or all at once and that all at once was the thing she was trying to avoid.
She went up on the first evening of it because not going was worse.
And it was a wash.
She stood in the middle of the hornbeams for eleven minutes with her hood down and she could not pick out one word.
Not one.
There were voices and voices and voices and every single one of them was inside every other one, and the whole thing had the acoustic character of a swimming pool.
She went up on all six evenings.
On the last one, walking out at the north end, with the noise thinning behind her, she heard one thing clearly.
It was three words and it was not hers and it was not Marta's, and it was in a voice she recognised immediately, and it was about something that had nothing to do with her at all.
Iva is twenty-four.

She has never told anybody what those three words were or whose voice it was, and the person is still alive and lives four hundred metres from her mother's house, and Iva has been perfectly ordinary with them for twelve years.
What she has said, to two people, is the other half of it — the part she worked out on the walk down that night and has not improved on since.
She had spent five months terrified that a wood was going to say her worst sentence out loud in front of everybody.
And the wood had said it, on all six evenings, along with about nine thousand other sentences, and it had been indistinguishable, and nobody had heard a thing.
And then on the last evening it had handed her, for free, three words that were somebody else's, and she has had to carry them ever since.
